To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the total number (epochs x images) of supervised weight updates needed to produce an adultlike primate ventral stream can be reduced by orders of magnitude using three complementary strategies.

we have reduced the number of supervised synaptic weight updates needed to produce an adult primate ventral stream by two orders of magnitude, by combining (1) a new, random, initial connectivity distribution that achieves 54% of a fully-trained model's brain match, (2) training only ~5.2% of the model synapses, and (3) using only ~2.1% of the model's supervised updates.

1) the number of supervised synaptic weight updates required to train a deep neural network to match the primate ventral visual stream can be reduced by two orders of magnitude; 2) the match to the adult ventral visual stream is achieved by training only 2% (or less) of the supervised synaptic weight updates; and 3) the match to an adult ventral stream can be achieved by training only ~ 5% of synapses.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of the primate ventral visual stream and the wiring up of this stream by evolution, development, and learning.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
these results demonstrate that a primate ventral stream can be produced by a deep neural network with a surprisingly small fraction of supervised synaptic weight updates.

the adult primate ventral visual stream is not a product of a single, precise, coordinated sequence of synaptic updates, but rather a result of a relatively simple, random, distributed, and sparse wiring of the brain.

the adult ventral primate visual system can be produced with a small number of supervised synaptic changes, even though the number of supervised updates is still large relative to the number of synapses in the brain.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ventral stream can be "wired" by evolution and learning to achieve ~80-95% of the match with adult ventral stream using only 0.02-2.0% of supervised weight updates (i.e. epochs and images).
the brain is a very efficient learner.
we have shown that the adult ventral visual stream can be modeled with only ~2% of the number of synaptic updates needed by the current best models.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in order to move closer to viable neurobiological hypotheses, it is critical to minimize the number of supervised updates needed to produce a model's match to primate ventral visual processing.

a model of the ventral visual system can be trained with far fewer supervised updates than previously thought, and that these supervised updates can be further reduced by exploiting the structure of the adult ventrals stream and by using random initial conditions.

, while the adult primate visual system may require millions of supervised synaptic updates for object recognition, the wiring up of a ventral stream that is functionally similar to the adult primate ventral stream may require far fewer supervised synaptic updates, perhaps as few as 100,000.
